title: Harp
region: Egypt, Late Second Intermediate Period–early New Kingdom

altText: An old wooden harp from ancient Egypt, long and slender, with a hollow body at one end and a curved neck rising from it. The wood is a dark, aged brown.

context: A wooden harp made in Egypt between about 1580 and 1295 B.C., from the end of the Second Intermediate Period into the early New Kingdom. It is about 120 cm long, a little over a meter, and about 14 cm high. Harps were among the instruments played in ancient Egypt.

descriptions.k: This is a very old harp from Egypt. It is made of wood and is longer than a big child's arm. It has a hollow body and a long neck. Imagine the strings. What sounds would they make?
descriptions.g12: This old wooden harp is about as long as a young child is tall. It was made in Egypt more than 3,000 years ago. It has a hollow body at one end and a neck that rises from it. Strings would have stretched between them. What song might have been played?
descriptions.g35: This wooden harp was made in ancient Egypt between about 1580 and 1295 B.C. It is about 120 centimeters long, so it is quite large. Musicians plucked the strings, which ran between the neck and the hollow body that made the sound louder. Look at the long, curved shape and the dark wood. What can the harp tell you about the people who made and played music?
descriptions.g68: Made around 1580–1295 B.C., this harp comes from a period when Egypt was changing from the Second Intermediate Period to the New Kingdom. About 120 cm long, it shows that harps were substantial instruments. Its long frame and hollow body worked together to hold strings and carry sound. What does the care taken in shaping the wood suggest about the importance of music in Egyptian life?
descriptions.g910: This harp is evidence of a musical tradition that has largely vanished in sound but survives in wood. Its size, about 1.2 meters, and its elegant curve show how engineering and design were combined. Surviving wood has darkened and perhaps lost strings and decoration, so we must infer what it once looked and sounded like. How does an incomplete instrument invite us to imagine performance?
descriptions.g1112: As a survival from the transition between the Second Intermediate Period and the early New Kingdom, this harp is valuable both as a musical instrument and as a witness to craft. Its length, about 120 cm, indicates a substantial instrument, and the wood bears the marks of age and loss. We can reconstruct sound only from other evidence, such as depictions in tombs and texts. The harp invites reflection on how museums display silent instruments, and on what is lost when objects survive without the practices that gave them life.

teacherNote.context: A large wooden harp from the end of the Second Intermediate Period or early New Kingdom. It is a rare survival of an Egyptian instrument; the record gives only its date, material, and size.
directions: Have students explore how different hollow containers change the sound of a plucked string.
Ask students to compare this harp with a harp shown in a painting and discuss what each can tell us.
Discuss how museums can help visitors imagine sounds that cannot be heard.
